knowledge_area.name: Industrial Fire & Explosion Intelligence
knowledge_area.description: An evidence-backed specialist system covering industrial fire and explosion hazards: flammable atmospheres, dust explosions, vapour cloud explosions, BLEVEs, ignition sources and control, hazardous area classification, and the UK and EU regimes that govern dangerous substances and major accident hazards. Answers are traceable to stored sources and are machine-checked for unsupported claims before they are returned.

failures.question: How many dust explosions occurred in Indonesian mills in 2024?
failures.answer: Dust clouds are a common source of explosions, causing an estimated 2,000 explosions annually in Europe.[13] The table lists notable incidents worldwide. [2] Husted Mill and Elevator DisasterJune 24, 1913Buffalo, New YorkUnited Statesgrain dust3380This workday afternoon explosion destroyed a grain elevator and mill complex. [4] Many common materials which are known to burn can generate a dust explosion, such as coal dust and sawdust. [6] A gigantic explosion of flour dust destroyed a mill in Minnesota on May 2, 1878, killing 14 workers at the Washburn A Mill and another four in adjacent buildings.[4] A similar problem occurs in sawmills and other places dedicated to woodworking. [6]

declared: This knowledge area is a seed built to prove the factory is repeatable. Its corpus is much smaller than Knowledge Area #001's and leans heavily on tertiary reference sources; treat its coverage as indicative, not complete.
ATEX, DSEAR and COMAH primary legal texts and the NFPA and IEC standards in this field are not fully held. Where a standard governs a topic the system can point at it but cannot quote it.

Flash points, explosive limits and autoignition temperatures are strongly dependent on substance, pressure, temperature and test method. Any single figure should be read as specific to the conditions its source reports.
